page.title: Identify a find
page.lead: Photograph it, then compare the closest matches with their dangerous look-alikes.
page.seoDescription: Identify wild mushrooms and plants from a photo, on your own device. Compare the closest matches with their toxic look-alikes.

coverage.note: Across verified records in Europe and the US.

guide.title: For a good match
guide.top: Top and cap: the whole specimen, filling the frame.
guide.under: Underside or stem base: gills, pores or ridges, or the base of the stem, where look-alikes differ.
guide.disagree: Matches disagree? Start over with a cut through the middle as the second photo.

disclaimer.aboveResults: These are possible matches, not a confirmed identification. A dangerous look-alike can be correct even when it is not the top result.
disclaimer.neverEat: Do not eat anything based on this app. A misidentification can be fatal. This tool never confirms that something is safe to eat.

results.heading: Possible matches
results.toxicBanner: One of these matches is toxic. Read every row before going further.
results.notInCatalog: Not in this app's catalog - no safety information
results.cautionGenus: Not in this app's catalog - its genus includes toxic species

mechanisms.amatoxin: Contains amatoxins, the same poisons as the death cap. Symptoms often start only 6 to 24 hours later. Then they ease off, which feels like recovery, before the liver fails. Often fatal.
mechanisms.gyromitrin: Contains gyromitrin, which the body converts to a toxin damaging the liver and nervous system. Can be fatal, and is not reliably destroyed by cooking.
mechanisms.muscarine: Contains high levels of muscarine, causing rapid sweating, salivation and collapse. Deaths have been recorded.
mechanisms.orellanine: Contains orellanine, which destroys the kidneys. Symptoms can take days to weeks to appear, long after the meal is forgotten.
mechanisms.isoxazole: Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, causing confusion, nausea and delirium. Rarely fatal but seriously unpleasant.
mechanisms.giIrritant: Causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea, sometimes for days. Not usually fatal, but dehydration can be dangerous.
mechanisms.colchicine: Contains colchicine. There is no antidote, symptoms are delayed, and a small amount can kill an adult.
mechanisms.cardiacGlycoside: Contains cardiac glycosides that disturb the heart rhythm. Can be fatal.
mechanisms.calciumOxalate: Contains needle-like calcium oxalate crystals that burn and swell the mouth and throat.
mechanisms.coniine: Contains coniine, the poison in hemlock. It paralyses the muscles used for breathing. Very small amounts are fatal.
mechanisms.tropane: Contains tropane alkaloids. A handful of berries can kill a child. Sweet taste offers no warning.
mechanisms.poorEdibility: Not dangerous, but poor eating and easily mistaken for something better.
mechanisms.bitter: Not poisonous, but so bitter that a single specimen ruins a whole dish.
mechanisms.taxine: Contains taxine alkaloids, which stop the heart. All parts except the red flesh of the aril are lethal, including the seed inside it. There is no home preparation that makes it safe.
mechanisms.immuneHaemolysis: Triggers an immune reaction that destroys red blood cells. It builds up over repeated meals, so having eaten it safely before is no reassurance at all. The poisoning can come after years of eating it.
mechanisms.nephrotoxic: Destroys the kidneys days after the meal, often needing dialysis. Cooking does not help.
mechanisms.rhabdomyolysis: Breaks down muscle tissue after repeated meals, which can stop the heart. Deaths are documented in people who had eaten it for years.
mechanisms.encephalopathy: Causes fatal brain inflammation, especially where kidney function is reduced. It caused a cluster of deaths in Japan among foragers who had eaten it safely before.
mechanisms.aconitine: One of the most toxic plants in Europe. Aconitine stops the heart, poisoning has followed skin contact alone, and there is no antidote.
mechanisms.cicutoxin: Causes violent seizures within an hour and is frequently fatal. A single root is enough. It is among the most poisonous plants in Europe.
mechanisms.ricin: The seeds contain one of the most lethal natural poisons known. A few chewed seeds can kill an adult, and there is no antidote.
mechanisms.cytisine: All parts, especially the seed pods, contain cytisine. Children have died after eating the pods, having taken them for peas.
mechanisms.grayanotoxin: Leaves, flowers and nectar contain grayanotoxins, which disturb heart rhythm. Honey made from the flowers has poisoned people.
mechanisms.veratrumAlkaloid: Collapses blood pressure and heart rate within hours. The young leaves are repeatedly mistaken for wild garlic, and those confusions have been fatal.
mechanisms.coprine: Contains coprine, which stops the body breaking down alcohol. Alcohol drunk in the hours before the meal or up to three days after it causes flushing, a racing heart, nausea and vomiting.
mechanisms.ptaquiloside: Contains ptaquiloside, which causes cancer (bracken is rated possibly carcinogenic to humans), and an enzyme that destroys vitamin B1. Cooking lowers the toxin but does not remove it.
mechanisms.phototoxic: Its sap burns skin in sunlight: painful blisters and scars that can last for years. Do not touch it with bare skin, and keep it away from the eyes.
mechanisms.atractyloside: Contains atractyloside, which shuts down the liver and kidneys. It has killed people who mistook it for wild artichoke or chewed its root.

checks.volva: Dig out the very base of the stem, below ground. If it sits in a sac-like bag or a swollen cup, take that as a serious warning.
checks.gillColour: Look at the gill colour, also on older mushrooms. Pure white gills on a mushroom with a stem call for great caution.
checks.gillAttachment: Look underneath. Real gills are thin blades, and you can lift one away from the next with a fingernail.
checks.gillVsRidges: True chanterelles have blunt, forking ridges that run down the stem. They don't have thin, crowded gills.
checks.sporePrint: Take a spore print. Lay the cap gills down on paper for a few hours, then check the colour of the powder it leaves.
checks.ringAndStem: Check the stem for a ring. See whether the ring slides up and down freely, and whether the stem below it has a pattern.
checks.overallSize: Look at the full-grown size. Some deadly look-alikes are much smaller than the edible mushroom they resemble.
checks.capWarts: Check the cap for patches or warts that you can rub off. Rain can wash them away, so a smooth cap proves nothing.
checks.cortina: On young mushrooms, look for a veil like a cobweb between the cap edge and the stem. On older ones, look for rusty-brown traces where it was.
checks.capStructure: Look at the head. A true morel has a regular honeycomb of pits. A false morel has irregular folds, like a brain.
checks.capAttachment: Check how the cap sits on the stem. It can be joined along its length, or hang free and attached only at the very top.
checks.hollowStem: Cut the mushroom in half from top to bottom. Check whether it is completely hollow inside.
checks.poreColour: Look at the pores under the cap. Red or orange tones are a warning sign.
checks.fleshBruising: Cut or press the flesh and watch whether it changes colour, and to which colour.
checks.fleshReddening: Check whether the flesh turns red where you have handled or damaged it.
checks.stemNetwork: Look for a raised net pattern on the stem, and note its colour.
checks.smell: Crush a leaf and smell it. Wild garlic smells strongly of garlic, and its deadly look-alikes don't.
checks.smellCompare: Smell a crushed leaf or freshly cut flesh and compare it with the edible species. An unexpected or unpleasant smell is a warning sign.
checks.leafArrangement: See how the leaves come up. Wild garlic leaves grow one by one from the base, each on its own stalk. Its look-alikes have leaves in pairs, wrapped around each other.
checks.leafShape: Look at the leaf outline and its veins, and check whether the base of the leaf is shaped like an arrowhead.
checks.stemMarkings: Check the stem. Is it hollow, ridged or blotched with purple? Does it smell unpleasant when you crush it?
checks.berryArrangement: See which way the berry clusters hang. They can droop below the branches or stand upright above the leaves.
checks.plantHabit: Check whether it is a woody shrub or a soft green plant that dies back every year.
checks.interiorPattern: Look at the skin, then cut it in half. A black truffle has a black skin of small pyramid-shaped warts. Inside it is dark, laced with fine white veins, and it smells strong and pleasant. An earthball has a yellowish to brown skin that is cracked or scaly, with a thick rind. Inside it is purple-black, and it smells sharp and unpleasant.
checks.berryColour: Look at the colour of the ripe berries. Elderberries for eating are purple-black. Red berries in upright, dome-shaped clusters belong to red elder, which is poisonous raw.
checks.flowerShape: Look at the flower. Violets have five uneven petals with a spur at the back. Lesser celandine has 8 to 12 shiny yellow petals.
checks.latexColour: Break a gill or the cap edge and watch the milk that comes out. Saffron milk caps bleed carrot-orange to wine-red milk. White or yellowing milk means a different milk cap.
checks.capMargin: Check whether the cap edge is rolled under and fringed with long, woolly hairs.
checks.capScales: Look at the cap. Is it covered in shaggy, upturned white scales, or is it smooth, grey-brown and finely grooved?
checks.fernStem: Look at the young stem. Ostrich fern fiddleheads are smooth, with brown papery scales and a deep U-shaped groove on the inside of the stem. Bracken is fuzzy, with a round stem and a top that splits into three.
checks.berryBloom: Sloes grow one by one on thorny blackthorn and have a dusty blue bloom that rubs off. Buckthorn berries are shiny black, grow in clusters along the twigs and have no bloom.
checks.jackOLantern: Look at the colour and how it grows. Oysters are grey, brown or cream and grow in shelves on dead wood, with no stem or a short one at the side. The jack-o'-lantern is bright orange right through. It grows in clumps with a real stem in the middle, often at the foot of oak or olive trees, and its gills run down that stem.
checks.angelWing: Look at the thickness, the colour and the wood. Angel wings are pure white, thin and fragile, and grow on rotting conifer wood. Oysters are thicker and fleshier, grey, brown or cream, and mostly grow on broadleaf wood.
checks.puffballInterior: Cut it in half from top to bottom. A giant puffball is pure white and soft all through, like marshmallow. Inside there is no outline of a cap, gills or stem. An earthball has a thick, scaly, yellowish skin. Inside it turns purple-black from the centre, marbled with white while it is young.
checks.sulphurTuft: Look at the colour, the stem and the spore print. Sulphur tuft is sulphur-yellow and grows in dense clumps with real stems. Its gills are greenish-yellow and turn purple-black, and its spore print is purple-brown. Oysters are grey, brown or cream and have almost no stem. Their gills are white to cream, and their spore print is white to pale lilac.
checks.jackOLanternChicken: Look underneath. Chicken of the woods has no gills, only tiny pores on a sulphur-yellow underside. It grows in overlapping shelves on trunks and stumps. The jack-o'-lantern has real orange gills that run down a real stem, and it grows in clumps at the foot of trees.
checks.scalyVase: Look at the shape and the cap. The scaly vase chanterelle is a tall trumpet, hollow down the middle, with coarse orange-red scales on top. Golden and Pacific chanterelles have a smooth, solid cap with no scales and no deep hollow.
checks.scaberStem: Look at the stem. Aspen boletes have rough dark scales on the stem and an orange cap, and their flesh darkens when you cut it. King boletes have a smooth stem with a fine pale net, and their flesh stays white.
checks.chestnutHusk: Look at the husk, the nut and the leaves. A sweet chestnut husk is covered in dense, fine spines as sharp as needles. Inside are usually two or three flat-sided nuts with a pointed tuft at the tip. The leaves are long, single and toothed. A horse chestnut husk is thick, with a few short, blunt spikes. Inside are one or two round, shiny conkers with no point. Its leaves are shaped like a hand.
checks.hedgeBerries: Look at where the red fruit hangs. Rose hips sit at the ends of thorny, woody stems, each with the dried remains of the flower on top. Black bryony, white bryony and bittersweet are soft climbers that wind through the hedge. They have bunches of small shiny berries and no thorns.
checks.asparagusShoot: Look at the shoot. Wild asparagus shoots come straight up from the ground next to last year's spiny plant with its needle-like leaves. Small triangular scales lie flat against the stem. Bryony shoots twine from the start and carry broad leaves or curling tendrils.
checks.hogweed: Look at the size and the stem. Giant hogweed grows 2 to 5 m tall. Its thick stem is blotched purple and covered in coarse bristles, its leaves are huge and deeply cut, and its flower heads are up to 50 cm across. Elder is a woody shrub. Masterwort grows knee- to waist-high and has broad leaflets in threes. Never touch hogweed with bare skin.
checks.pimpernel: Look at the stem and the flowers. Scarlet pimpernel has square, hairless stems, black dots under the leaves and small orange-red or blue flowers. Chickweed has round stems with a single line of hairs and small white star-shaped flowers with deeply split petals.
checks.spurgeSap: Break a stem. Spurges bleed a white, milky sap that burns skin and eyes, and they have small green cup-shaped flowers. Chickweed never has milky sap, and its flowers are white stars.
checks.nightshadeFlower: Look at the flowers and the fruit. Black nightshade has small white star-shaped flowers with a yellow cone in the middle, and green berries that turn black. Amaranth has no petals at all, only dense spikes of tiny green or reddish flowers.
checks.thornApple: Look at the leaves, flowers and fruit. Thorn apple has big, coarsely toothed leaves that smell unpleasant, large white or violet trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods. Amaranth leaves are smooth-edged ovals, and its flowers are dense spikes with no petals.
checks.thistleRosette: Look at the stem and the flower. Wild artichoke grows a tall, leafy stem with big purple flower heads. Never eat a thistle rosette without a stem, or a thistle root. The deadly Chamaeleon gummifer (Atractylis gummifera) flowers flat in the middle of its rosette and has a thick root with sticky white sap.
checks.arumLeaf: Look at the leaf and its veins. Lords-and-ladies has large, shiny, arrow-shaped leaves with a net of veins, often with dark spots, and a hooded flower spike in spring. Sorrel leaves are smaller and matt, with sharp lobes pointing backwards. Violet leaves are heart-shaped with wavy edges. Never taste a leaf to check.
checks.plantainVeins: Look at the leaf veins. Plantain leaves have five to nine parallel veins that pull out like strings when you tear the leaf. The leaves are smooth to slightly hairy. Foxglove leaves are soft and downy, with a net of veins, toothed edges and a winged stalk.

critical.lepiotaMacrolepiota: Deadly Lepiota species are among the most dangerous look-alikes for the Parasol mushroom, and this was the single most frequent mistake in our testing. A true Parasol is large, with a movable ring and a snakeskin-patterned stem. Small specimens with a plain stem should be left alone even if they look right.
critical.trufflePair: Both a truffle and a poisonous false truffle are among the matches. From the outside they are genuinely hard to tell apart. Cut the find open before anything else: marbled pale veins mean truffle, a solid dark interior means false truffle.
critical.angelWingPair: Both an oyster mushroom and the angel wing are among the matches. The angel wing has caused fatal brain inflammation. It is thinner, pure white, and grows on conifer wood: check the wood and the flesh thickness before anything else.
critical.veratrumPair: Both wild garlic and white hellebore are among the matches. This confusion has killed people. Crush a leaf: wild garlic smells strongly of garlic, hellebore does not. Hellebore leaves are also strongly ribbed and grow alternately up the stem.
critical.inkCapAlcohol: Both a shaggy mane and the common ink cap are among the matches. The common ink cap reacts violently with alcohol, even alcohol drunk days after the meal. A shaggy mane is tall, white and covered in shaggy scales; the common ink cap is smaller, grey-brown and smooth. If in doubt, leave it, and never drink alcohol with ink caps.
critical.matsutakeSmithiana: Both a matsutake and Amanita smithiana are among the matches. Amanita smithiana destroys the kidneys and has been picked for matsutake in the Pacific Northwest. Smell it and dig out the whole base: a matsutake smells spicy, like cinnamon. Amanita smithiana does not, and its base swells and then tapers into the soil like a root, ringed with white scraps of veil.
critical.puffballPair: Both a giant puffball and a poisonous look-alike are among the matches. Cut it in half from top to bottom before anything else. A puffball is pure white and even all the way through. A purple-black interior means an earthball; the outline of a cap, gills and stem means a young Amanita, which can be deadly.
critical.rampsPair: Both ramps and a poisonous look-alike are among the matches. Lily of the valley, false hellebore and autumn crocus have similar leaves, and all three are toxic. Crush a leaf: ramps smell strongly of onion or garlic, the look-alikes do not. Lily of the valley has two leaves wrapped around one stalk; false hellebore leaves are deeply pleated and climb a stout stem.
critical.fiddleheadBracken: Both ostrich fern fiddleheads and bracken are among the matches. Bracken causes cancer and is not a fiddlehead to eat. Ostrich fern fiddleheads are smooth, with brown papery scales and a deep U-shaped groove inside the stem; bracken is fuzzy and branches in three at the top.
